title: How To Teach Routines
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin lays out a six-step method for teaching classroom routines so thoroughly that students perform them correctly and independently every time. The steps progress from teacher modeling correct and incorrect versions, to individual student modeling, to small-group modeling, to whole-class practice with a 'go' signal, and finally to live daily use. He stresses holding students to exacting standards throughout, sending them back to redo a routine at the smallest deviation, since these details resonate most with students. Perfection, he clarifies, doesn't mean robotic or militaristic execution — routines can still be casual — but they must be performed as taught. He closes by describing routines as a vehicle for transferring a broader culture of excellence across every part of the school day.
points: Teaching a routine should progress through six steps: teacher modeling right and wrong ways, individual student modeling, group modeling, whole-class practice, and live use.
Holding students to an exacting standard at each stage — sending them back to redo even small deviations — is what makes routines stick.
Modeling how not to perform a routine, even exaggerated for effect, underscores the absurdity of misbehaving in a peaceful classroom.
Perfection in a routine doesn't mean robotic execution; routines can remain casual as long as they're performed as taught.
Consistently taught routines transfer a broader culture of excellence across every subject and part of the school day.
quotes: The key is to teach routines in a way that compels your students to perform them correctly—and without your input—every single time.
Start your lesson seated at a student’s desk—or wherever the routine is to begin—and simply show your class what you want them to do.
Call upon your experience in the past and model how not to perform the routine. It’s okay to have fun with it.
If you see even the smallest mistake, the smallest deviation from the script, have the student go back and do it again.
Perfection does not mean robotic or militaristic. It simply means performing the routines as taught.
Pushing in chairs, lining up for lunch, behaving politely, dividing fractions . . . it’s all the same steady drip, drip, drip of excellence you require of your students.
